title: The boy who feared the fire
hook: tradition says a boy told Nanak small sticks catch fire first, so death takes the young too; he became Baba Buddha

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rabab, handed to Mardana's son so the music wouldn't stop: keep playing. Today, a boy with a hard question.

Kids ask the questions adults have learned to step around. Where do people go when they die? Will you die? Will I? Sometimes the grown-ups change the subject, or say, not for a long, long time. Sikh tradition keeps a story about a boy who asked that question and didn't accept the easy answer, because he'd already worked out the hard one himself, watching his mother at the stove. Nanak, the story says, was so struck that he gave the boy a new name.
screen: `WILL I DIE TOO?` → `THE EASY ANSWER.` → `A BOY WHO WORKED IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here is the story as tradition tells it. Nanak was staying near a village, and a boy who grazed the village cattle began coming to him every day, bringing milk, sitting nearby, listening. One day Nanak asked why a boy his age spent his time with holy talk instead of play. The boy answered with something he'd seen at home. When my mother lights the fire, she puts in the small sticks first, and they catch before the big logs. So who can say death will wait for the old? It takes the young too. Nanak, the story goes, said: you are young in years, but you speak like an old man. And he called him Buddha: old one. The boy grew up to be Baba Buddha, the revered elder Sikhs remember serving the Gurus who came after Nanak. His wisdom came from no book, but from a kitchen fire and a habit of noticing. And he wasn't morbid. His fear didn't make him hide; it made him come and sit and listen, every day. Being called old, in this story, is high praise. And the grown-up in the story didn't brush him off. A Guru took a cowherd boy's question seriously enough to answer it with a name he would carry for life.
screen: `A COWHERD BOY BRINGS MILK.` · `SMALL STICKS CATCH FIRST.` · `YOU SPEAK LIKE AN OLD MAN.` · `THE BOY BECOMES BABA BUDDHA.` · then, large: `WISE WHEN YOUNG.`

segments.voice: Let the boy's question sit with you, seriously but not gloomily: no one is promised a long life. Then gently ask what you'd want today to hold if it were the measure, one person to speak to, one thing to finish or forgive, and rest with that. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Baba Buddha, the name Nanak gave the young cowherd who, in the story, saw small sticks catch first and spoke of death taking the young, not only the old.
Your line: wise when young. Wisdom can start at a kitchen fire. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Baba Buddha as a revered elder of the early community, and the story of the boy and the kindling is a sakhi told to children.

chat.says: Why did Guru Nanak call a little boy 'old one'?
options: The boy saw small sticks catch fire first, and said death takes the young too.
The boy had gray hair even as a child, so the name was a gentle joke.
He was the oldest child in his family, so the name was a family title.
chat.meaning: He spoke like an old man: small sticks catch first, so death can take the young. Nanak named him Buddha, old one.

Baba Buddha.meaning: the revered elder the cowherd boy grew up to be

Gurus.meaning: the Sikh Gurus: Nanak and the teachers who came after him

notes: Tradition gives the boy's name as Bura and the village as Kathu Nangal (near Amritsar); both omitted from the voice. Confirm whether to include.
